17-075.r: CECRI (Central Electrochemical Research Institute) → Karaikudi, Tamil Nadu; founded 1948, dedicated 14 January 1953 by Dr. S. Radhakrishnan; efforts of Alagappa Chettiar, Nehru, Bhatnagar.

17-076.r: Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru → established 1909 with support of Jamshedji Tata.

17-077.r: RKCL (Rajasthan Knowledge Corporation Limited) → Rajasthan government company to plan and regulate IT skill needs of the 21st century.

17-078.r: NCESS (National Centre for Earth Science Studies) → Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala; set up by Kerala government as CESS in 1978; studies land, sea and atmosphere.

17-079.r: Wrong pair: Antarctic Study Centre – Bangalore. NCAOR is at Vasco da Gama, Goa. Correct: NIO – Goa; INCOIS – Hyderabad; NIOT – Chennai.

17-080.r: Central Institute of Indian Languages → Mysuru, not Mumbai. Correct: ARIES – Nainital; College of Defence Management – Secunderabad; IISc – Bengaluru.

17-081.r: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies → Varanasi; IGIDR → Mumbai; NIMHANS → Bengaluru; CIEFL (now English and Foreign Languages University) → Hyderabad.

17-082.r: Indian Institute of Naturopathy and Yogic Science → Bengaluru, Karnataka.

17-083.r: Hi-Tec City → Hyderabad; Science City → Calcutta; Rocket Launching Centre → Thumba (Thiruvananthapuram); Central Drug Research Institute → Lucknow.

17-084.r: Carbon microphone → best used in telephones (early telephone repeaters made long-distance calls possible); converts sound to electrical signal and can amplify.

17-085.r: Laws of planetary motion → Johannes Kepler (early 1600s); every planet moves round the Sun in an elliptical orbit.

17-086.r: Soleckshaw → solar rickshaw: eco-friendly tricycle run by pedal plus a battery charged by solar energy; developed by CSIR scientists.

17-087.r: Bibliometry → an information management tool; quantitative statistical technique to measure production and spread of knowledge.

17-088.r: Cytotron → device that produces artificial climate (also trade name of an RFQMR tissue-repair device by CARD, Bengaluru).

17-089.r: First engineering college of Asia (British Empire) → Roorkee College, 1847; renamed Thomson College of Civil Engineering (1854); university status 1948.

17-090.r: Metric (decimal) system in India → 1 April 1957; coins minted 1957–1964 were called 'Naya Paisa'.

17-091.r: Tachyon (Greek 'rapid') → hypothetical particle that travels faster than light.

17-092.r: John C. Mather → 2006 Physics Nobel (with George Smoot); Michael Griffin → NASA Administrator (2005–2009); Paul G. Allen → Microsoft co-founder; Piers Sellers → spacewalker.

17-093.r: Raja Ramanna → led India's first peaceful nuclear test team (Rajasthan); Padma Vibhushan 1975; Union Minister of State for Defence 1990; wrote on Raga and Western music. All true.

17-094.r: Water jet technology → cuts materials with very high-pressure water (or water with abrasive); used mainly in drilling of mines and aeronautics.

17-095.r: Laser beam → used in many treatments: shrinking tumours, relieving cancer symptoms, removing kidney stones, repairing detached retina, improving vision.
17-095.c: The book gives no single answer (*): lasers treat cancer, eye and kidney problems, so more than one option fits.

17-096.r: Dry ice → solid carbon dioxide (CO2); Gene therapy → treating blood diseases; Cryonics → freezing bodies to revive later; Cobalt-60 → cancer treatment.

17-097.r: Adobe → software (multimedia) company, not hardware. Correct: Y2K – computer; arthritis – uric acid; noise pollution – decibel.

17-098.r: True: carbon monoxide causes more air pollution (plants do not absorb it). Homeopathy → Samuel Hahnemann, not Johns Hopkins; evolution → Charles Darwin, not Newton.

17-099.r: Atom bomb principle → nuclear fission; Otto Hahn and F. Strassmann (1939) split Uranium-235 with slow neutrons, releasing huge energy.

17-101.r: Nagasaki bomb 'Fat Man' (9 August 1945) → plutonium; Hiroshima bomb 'Little Boy' (6 August 1945) → uranium.
17-101.h: Fat (plump) Man = Plutonium; Little Boy = Uranium.

17-102.r: First 3D television broadcast → USA: station KECA, Los Angeles, 29 April 1953, an episode of 'Space Patrol' (viewers wore Polaroid 3D glasses).

17-103.r: True: liquid crystals' main use is digital display (LCD); a modem links a computer to a phone line. False: NIO at Coimbatore; Virginis-70 as video recorder.

17-104.r: Liquid crystals → used in wrist watches, display devices, pocket calculators and portable computers (all of the above).

17-105.r: Rare earth elements (europium, terbium, yttrium) → phosphors with phosphorescent properties give colours on flat TV screens and monitors; Statement II explains I.

17-106.r: OLED (organic film emits light with current) advantages over LCD → made on flexible plastic, roll-up displays in clothing, transparent displays. All three true.

17-107.r: 1080p at 16:9 aspect ratio → 1920 × 1080 pixels, called Full HD (FHD).
17-107.h: 1080p: the 1080 is the vertical pixel count; width is 1920.

17-108.r: Radiator → heat exchanger that cools internal combustion engines of vehicles (also locomotives, piston aircraft).

17-109.r: Mobiles → connectivity of people; automobiles → mobility of people. Sensitivity is not the change.

17-110.r: Manav → India's first 3D-printed humanoid robot, by Diwakar Vaish at A-SET Training and Research Institutes (December 2014); 2-foot, 2-kilogram research robot.

17-111.r: Optimus → Tesla's humanoid robot; prototype revealed by Elon Musk in October 2022; shares AI and sensors with Tesla Autopilot.

17-112.r: Replacing jobs (job losses) → a disadvantage of robots. Advantages: help people with disabilities, work in dangerous places, never tire.

17-113.r: AICRA (All India Council for Robotics and Automation) → not-for-profit apex body for robotics and automation standards in India; set up 2014.

18-001.r: Father of Modern Chemistry → Antoine Lavoisier (French); found oxygen's role in combustion; named oxygen (1778) and hydrogen (1783); first extensive list of elements.

18-002.r: Dalton's atomic theory explained the law of conservation of mass, law of constant composition and law of multiple proportions; not radioactivity.

18-003.r: First model of atomic structure → J.J. Thomson's 'plum pudding' model (late 19th century): positive sphere with electrons embedded like plums.

18-004.r: Nucleus → small, dense, positively charged centre of an atom, made of protons and neutrons.

18-005.r: Atomic nucleus → protons and neutrons (nucleons); electrons surround the nucleus.
18-005.t: Electrons are not in the nucleus.

18-007.r: Wrong: electrons inside the nucleus. Nucleus holds protons and neutrons; electrons revolve around it; equal positive and negative charges make the atom neutral.

18-009.r: Photon → not part of an atom; it is an energy packet of light. Atom = protons, neutrons, electrons.

18-010.r: Native element → material made of a single type of atom; a compound has two or more types of atoms.

18-011.r: Atomic nucleus → discovered 1911 by Ernest Rutherford, interpreting the 1909 Geiger–Marsden gold foil experiment; proton–neutron model by Dmitri Ivanenko, 1932.

18-012.r: Order: electron (1897, J.J. Thomson) → proton (1919, Rutherford) → neutron (1932, Chadwick) → pi meson (1947, Cecil Powell).
18-012.h: E-P-N-Pi: Electron, Proton, Neutron, then pi meson.

18-013.r: Neutron (no electric charge) → discovered by James Chadwick in 1932 by bombarding beryllium with high-speed particles.

18-014.r: Deuteron (one proton + one neutron) → not a basic sub-atomic particle; the three main ones are protons, neutrons, electrons.

18-015.r: Electron–positron → particle–antiparticle pair; positron (antielectron) has the electron's mass but positive charge.

18-016.r: Zero mass → neutrino; fractional charge → quark; fractional spin (½) → positron; integral spin → phonon.

18-017.r: Fundamental (elementary) particle, with no sub-structure → quark. Fundamental fermions: quarks, leptons and their antiparticles; neutron, proton, π-meson are not fundamental.

18-018.r: Higgs boson → 'God Particle' (name from Leon Lederman's 1993 book); force-carrier of the Higgs field, which gives mass to particles like electrons and quarks.

18-019.r: 'God particle' → Higgs boson; proposed 1964, confirmed 14 March 2013; Peter Higgs and François Englert won the 2013 Physics Nobel.

18-021.r: Higgs boson discovery → helps explain why elementary particles have mass (only statement 1); not matter transfer or better fission fuel.

18-022.r: Neutron → no charge. Alpha particle (+2) and proton are positive; electron is negative.

18-023.r: Neutrino → zero charge, very small (maybe zero) mass; among the most abundant particles, very hard to detect. Positron and α-particle are positive, electron negative.

18-024.r: Alpha particle → 2 protons + 2 neutrons = helium nucleus; charge +2; mass equals a helium atom's nucleus.

18-026.r: Hydrogen → its protium isotope has no neutron (deuterium has one, tritium two); atomic number of hydrogen is 1.

18-027.r: Beta particles → high-energy electrons (or positrons) from the nucleus, negatively charged, negligible mass. Alpha → positive; gamma → photons with no mass or charge.

18-028.r: Alpha rays → positively charged particles emitted by radioactive elements; they are helium nuclei.
18-028.t: Beta rays (electrons) and cathode rays are negative, not positive.

18-029.r: Order of filling orbitals → Aufbau principle: the atom is 'built up' by adding electrons to the most stable orbitals first.
18-029.t: Hund's rule and Pauli's exclusion principle are other rules; the filling order is Aufbau.

18-030.r: Magnetic quantum number (m) → orientation of the orbital; third of four quantum numbers (principal, azimuthal, magnetic, spin).
18-030.t: Principal number gives size, azimuthal gives shape, magnetic gives orientation.

18-031.r: Mass number = protons + neutrons; protons = electrons = 18, neutrons = 20 → 18 + 20 = 38.

18-032.r: Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons = 2 + 2 = 4; electrons are not counted.

18-034.r: Neutrons in Pu-242 = mass number 242 − 94 protons = 148.

18-035.r: Isotopes → same number of protons (atomic number Z), different number of neutrons (mass number A). Unstable isotopes = radioisotopes.

18-036.r: Isotopes → same atomic number, different mass number (e.g. Oxygen-16, 17, 18; Chlorine-35, 37). Protium, deuterium, tritium are isotopes of hydrogen, not carbon.

18-040.r: Isotones (isoneutronic) → same neutron number, different proton number; carbon-14, nitrogen-15, oxygen-16 each have 8 neutrons.
18-040.t: Isotopes share protons; isobars share mass number; isotones share neutrons.

18-041.r: Radioactivity measured by → Geiger–Muller (Geiger) counter; detects alpha, beta, gamma radiation by ionisation in a Geiger-Muller tube.

18-042.r: Radioactivity → discovered 1896 by French scientist Henri Becquerel while working with phosphorescent materials.

19-001.r: Physical change → form changes, composition does not; e.g. sugar dissolving in water (sugar can be recovered). Burning candle, curd from milk, silver blackening → chemical.

19-002.r: Water changing into vapour → physical change.

19-003.r: Cooking (softening) vegetables → chemical change (irreversible change in composition). Prism dispersion, drying soil, dissolving salt → physical changes.

19-004.r: Souring of milk → chemical change; crystallisation of sodium chloride and melting of ice → physical changes.

19-005.r: Ripening of fruit, setting of cement, burning of coal → all chemical and exothermic changes, so no odd one (None of the above).

19-006.r: Reactions are faster at higher temperature because molecules move faster (more kinetic energy); both A and R true, R explains A.

19-007.r: Book's answer: heat. It explains via hydrolysis, where ions of a dissolved salt combine with water to form an acidic or basic solution.
19-007.c: Splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen absorbs energy; it does not give out heat. The book's answer rests on salt hydrolysis, not on decomposing water.

19-008.r: Pasteurisation → milk heated for a set time, then cooled suddenly; Louis Pasteur (1864) found heating beer and wine kills spoilage bacteria.

19-009.r: Pasteurisation → sterilisation of milk: heating kills harmful microbes (moderate heat for 30 minutes or higher heat for 15 seconds); named after Louis Pasteur.

19-010.r: Pasteurisation → partial sterilisation of milk, wine, fruit juice (Louis Pasteur, 1864), not tea. Desalination – sea water, reverse osmosis – potable water, denaturation – proteins are correct.

19-011.r: Phosphatase test → for milk and dairy products: alkaline phosphatase (ALP) in raw milk is destroyed by proper heating, so the test checks pasteurisation.
19-011.c: The phosphatase test is the standard check of milk pasteurisation, so (a) Milk is the textbook answer; the book prints (d) because MPPSC's final key accepted it, citing uses for water and tea.

19-012.r: Impurities in a liquid → raise its boiling point.

19-013.r: Salt + ice (freezing mixture) → temperature below 0°C because salt lowers, not raises, the freezing point. A true, R false.

19-014.r: Amount of solute per unit volume or mass of solution/solvent → concentration of solution.

19-015.r: Ideal solution → enthalpy of mixing (ΔH) is zero; solute–solvent forces equal solute–solute and solvent–solvent forces.

19-016.r: Salt in water → raises boiling point, lowers freezing point; methyl alcohol in water → lowers boiling point (hydrogen bonding). Both true.

19-017.r: Conductivity of a strong electrolyte → decreases (slightly) on dilution; it dissociates fully, so dilution only spreads the same ions over more volume.

19-018.r: Milk → emulsion (oil-in-water): a colloid of two immiscible liquids, one dispersed in the other.

19-020.r: Honey → not a colloid (supercooled liquid: glucose crystals in fructose solution). Milk, blood, ice cream are colloids.

19-021.r: Fog → colloid of liquid in gas: water vapour condenses on dust particles as tiny droplets that stay suspended in air.

19-022.r: Salt solution in water → homogeneous (same composition throughout). A mixture with different composition throughout is heterogeneous, so R is false.

19-023.r: Unsaturated sugar solution (100 g sugar in half litre water) → volume stays the same, as per the book; mass, density, concentration change.

19-024.r: Water enters roots from soil → osmosis via root hairs (diffusion of water through a semi-permeable membrane).

19-025.r: Salt on cut cucumber → water comes out by osmosis, as the outside becomes more concentrated than the cell sap.

19-026.r: Osmosis → solvent moves from dilute to concentrated solution; reverse osmosis → pressure applied on the concentrated solution. Both statements wrong.
19-026.t: The statements swap the directions: solvent never goes from concentrated to dilute in osmosis.

19-027.r: Solvent flowing through a semipermeable membrane from pure solvent into solution → osmosis, not reverse osmosis. Only (1) true.

19-028.r: Distillation → purifies liquids (liquid impurities); sublimation and crystallisation → remove solid impurities.

19-029.r: Chromatography → separates components of a mixture by differential partitioning between mobile and stationary phases.

19-030.r: Solid camphor → camphor vapour directly = sublimation.

19-031.r: Camphor, naphthalene, dry ice (solid CO2) vanish in air → sublimation: solid directly to gas, skipping liquid.

19-033.r: Sand + naphthalene mixture → separated by sublimation, as naphthalene turns directly into gas on heating.

19-034.r: Oxidation numbers: Ca in CaO = +2; Al in NaAlH4 = +3; Mn in MnO2 = +4; S in H2SO4 = +6. Sum in a compound is zero.

19-035.r: Catalytic promoters, homogeneous catalysts (same phase) and heterogeneous catalysts (different phase) all speed up reactions → none slows them.

19-036.r: Exothermic: dilution of an acid (H2SO4) and quicklime (CaO) reacting with water to form Ca(OH)2. Evaporation of water and sublimation of camphor are not.

19-037.r: Displacement: copper in silver nitrate → copper (more reactive) displaces silver: Cu + 2AgNO3 → Cu(NO3)2 + 2Ag.
19-037.h: A more reactive metal pushes a less reactive one out of its salt.

19-038.r: Corrosion → gradual decay of metals by air or chemicals: brown rust on iron, green coating on copper, black coating on silver (all three).

20-001.r: 2019 → UNESCO's International Year of the Periodic Table, marking 150 years since Mendeleev's periodic table (1869).

20-002.r: Down a group: electron affinity decreases (A false); atomic radius increases as electron shells are added (R true).

20-003.r: Across a period, ionisation potential increases (statement 1 wrong); down a group, electron affinity decreases as atomic weight rises (true). Only statement 2 correct.

20-004.r: Oxides of Group 3 and 4 → both basic and acidic (amphoteric: react as base and as acid).

20-006.r: Earth's crust/soil by mass → oxygen 46.60% (most), then silicon 27.72%, aluminium 8.13%, iron 5.00%, calcium 3.65%.
20-006.h: Order O, Si, Al, Fe, Ca: 'Oh Sir, All Fe(e)s Ca(ncelled)'.

20-008.r: Most abundant on Earth's surface after oxygen → silicon; discovered by J.J. Berzelius (1824); name from Latin 'silex'; used in semiconductor chips.

20-009.r: Most common element in the Universe → hydrogen (about ¾ of all matter; helium most of the rest). In Earth's crust → oxygen (46.6%).

20-010.r: 118 elements identified so far; on 28 November 2016 IUPAC approved names Nihonium, Moscovium, Tennessine, Oganesson.
20-010.c: No option says 118, but (d) 100 is clearly the nearest; about ninety elements occur naturally on Earth, and 118 are known in all.

20-011.r: Diamond → purest crystalline form of carbon, an element. Sand (silicon, oxygen), marble (calcium, carbon, oxygen), sugar (carbon, hydrogen, oxygen) are compounds.

20-013.r: Types of elements → metals, non-metals, metalloids (semimetals). 'Gases' is not a type; gaseous elements like hydrogen, neon are non-metals.

20-014.r: First artificially produced element → Technetium (Tc, atomic number 43), isolated by Carlo Perrier and Emilio Segre in 1937.
20-014.h: Technetium from Greek 'technetos' = artificial: the first man-made element.

21-001.r: Smelting → ore reduced at high temperature, giving metal in a fused (molten) state.

21-002.r: Configuration 2, 8, 8, 2 → calcium, a metal: it loses two electrons to reach a noble gas configuration.

21-003.r: Na+ → not a true electrophile (stable octet, no low-energy vacant orbital). Electrophiles are electron-deficient species that accept electrons, like H+ and BF3.

21-004.r: Most reactive metal among sodium, calcium, iron, potassium → potassium; reacts vigorously with air and water; larger atom, lower ionisation energy than sodium.

21-005.r: Food cans are coated with tin, not zinc → zinc is more reactive and could react with food acids; tin is less reactive and safer.

21-006.r: Paramagnetism (weak attraction to a magnetic field) → platinum among nickel, mercury, iron, platinum.
21-006.t: Nickel and iron are ferromagnetic (strongly attracted), not paramagnetic.

21-007.r: Paramagnetic and ferromagnetic pair → Cu²⁺ (paramagnetic, partly attracted) and Gd (gadolinium, ferromagnetic: aligned unpaired spins, keeps magnetism).

21-008.r: Lightest metal → lithium (density 0.534 g/cc); heaviest (densest) metal → osmium (22.61 g/cc).
21-008.t: Mercury (13.534 g/cc) is lighter than osmium.

21-009.r: Hardest metal → tungsten; hardest natural material overall → diamond (a non-metal).

21-010.r: Diamond → hardest, least compressible and best thermal conductor among natural materials.

21-011.r: Hardest naturally occurring substance on Earth → diamond; wurtzite boron nitride (formed in volcanic eruptions) is believed harder, handling 18% more stress.

21-012.r: Nichrome (nickel-chromium alloy) → very hard and very ductile; high resistivity and melting point; used in resistance wire.

21-013.r: Heaviest natural element → uranium (atomic number 92); Uranium-238 has 92 protons and 146 neutrons; density 19.05 g/cm³.

21-015.r: Heaviest metal among gold, silver, mercury, platinum → platinum (density 21.09 g/cm³).

21-016.r: Costliest material per gram → endohedral fullerene (about $167 million); californium-252 about $27 million; tritium $30,000; rhodium $58.
21-016.c: The book gives no single answer (*); its table shows the costliest material, endohedral fullerene, is not a metal.

21-017.r: Pearl → mainly calcium carbonate (aragonite, 82–86%), conchiolin (a protein binder, 10–14%) and 2–4% water.

21-020.r: Rubies and sapphires → aluminium oxide (Al2O3); gem forms of corundum coloured by trace impurities.

21-021.r: Sapphire (ruby) → Al2O3, aluminium oxide; a gem variety of the mineral corundum.

21-022.r: Sodium is stored under kerosene to keep it from air's oxygen (it reacts strongly, giving much heat); it does not melt in air. A true, R false.

21-024.r: Yellow street lamps → sodium vapour; mercury vapour lamps give white light.

21-025.r: Sodium vapour street lamps → give monochromatic yellow light that does not split through water droplets; less light pollution than mercury-vapour lamps.

21-026.r: Gold → found in the native (free) state as it is least reactive; silver and platinum also occur native.

21-027.r: Noble metals → resist corrosion and occur pure in nature (gold, platinum group metals). Uranium and lead are not noble metals. Only 1 correct.

21-028.r: Gold dissolves only in aqua regia → hydrochloric acid + nitric acid in 3:1 ratio; unaffected by air, water and single acids.
21-028.c: The book gives no single answer (*): gold dissolves in aqua regia (HCl + HNO3), and no option names it.

21-029.r: Pure gold → 24 carat; 18 carat = 18 parts in 24 = 75% gold. Pure gold is soft, so it is alloyed for jewellery.

21-030.r: 'White metal' → alloys (lead with lithium, or cadmium, bismuth, zinc) used as a base for plated silverware; book's answer is (e) None/More than one.

21-031.r: Minerals → naturally occurring inorganic solids with definite chemical composition and physical properties.

21-032.r: Ilmenite (FeTiO3) → titanium-iron oxide, the main ore of titanium and source of titanium dioxide; found along the Indian coast.

21-033.r: Talc (soapstone) → hydrated magnesium silicate; softest mineral, 1 on Mohs scale (diamond = 10); loose form is talcum powder.

21-034.r: Quicklime (burnt lime) → calcium oxide, CaO: white, caustic, alkaline solid.
21-034.t: Limestone is CaCO3; slaked lime is Ca(OH)2.
